meta.title: MCPCA · Build, update and study your Moodle courses inside Teams, Copilot, ChatGPT or Claude
meta.description: MCPCA is a plugin for Moodle, the platform behind most online training in universities, schools, healthcare organisations and training providers. Teachers, trainers, instructional designers and learners can build and consult courses by talking to the AI assistant they already use.

hero.badge: Moodle plugin · Teams and Copilot · ChatGPT · Claude
hero.lead: Moodle is **the most widely used distance-learning platform**: universities, schools, healthcare organisations and training providers all run on it.
hero.lead2: [[MCPCA]] _connects_ Moodle to AI assistants: from existing material or from scratch, describe a page, a quiz or a whole course, typed or spoken, and ==find it ready on the platform==, without Moodle's editor and with nothing to install. Students, in turn, query their own courses for clarification and revision.

flow.caption: Everything inside your organisation's own infrastructure

what.title: What it is, without the jargon
what.lead: AI assistants such as Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude can hold a conversation, but **they know nothing about the content of your organisation's courses and cannot act on it**. [[MCPCA]] is the missing link.

cards.title: A plugin for Moodle
cards.text: Moodle is the open source platform behind **a large share of online training, in Italy and worldwide**: courses, materials, assessments and activity tracking. MCPCA installs inside it like any other component: **no extra servers, no external services**.

cards.title: It speaks the language of AI assistants
cards.text: It uses MCP (_Model Context Protocol_), an open standard adopted by AI assistants and agents such as _Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude_. The assistant can therefore read and write in the courses published on Moodle **for which the signed-in user holds the relevant permissions**, and _only with that user's explicit approval_.

cards.title: Under Moodle's permissions
cards.text: Each person signs in with their own institutional account. The plugin performs only the operations that person could perform through Moodle's web interface: **a teacher creates and edits in the courses they run, a learner consults the ones they are enrolled in**.

what.glossary_title: Four terms you will come across

glossary.def: The most widely used open source e-learning platform, run by universities, schools, healthcare organisations and training providers. If your organisation has a _training portal_, a _distance-learning platform_ or an _e-learning portal_, it is almost certainly built on Moodle.

An open standard through which an AI assistant (or agent) asks an application “what can you do?” and then asks it to do those things. It is the same technology Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude use to connect to SharePoint, Jira or Google Drive.
The Microsoft tool used to build an assistant and publish it in Teams and in Microsoft 365 Copilot. It is included in many licences already held by universities, schools and companies.
The Microsoft identity service through which staff and learners already sign in to Teams and email. MCPCA uses it to recognise who is in the conversation.

sectors.title: Anywhere training happens at a distance
sectors.lead: **The plugin knows nothing about your sector: it knows Moodle.** MCPCA grew out of a university teaching need, but the same tools apply wherever teaching content has to be produced and maintained online.

items.title: Universities and higher technical institutes
items.text: Degree programmes, labs, specialisation courses. Materials to refresh every academic year, mid-term and final exams to renew for every session, _different_ for every student.

items.title: Schools
items.text: Virtual classrooms, remedial work, homework and tests. The teacher describes the lesson and finds it published, without working through the platform's configuration screens.

items.title: Healthcare organisations, public and private
items.text: Staff training, procedures and protocols, continuing medical education. **Completion tracking** and **assessments that differ for every participant** meet the requirements of this setting directly.

items.title: Accredited training providers
items.text: Certified courses and asynchronous distance learning, where every module has to be documented, passed and recorded. Building and replicating each run becomes a matter of minutes.

items.title: Companies
items.text: Onboarding, workplace safety, updates on products and procedures. _Whoever writes the content is usually the person who does the job, not an expert in the platform._

items.title: Public bodies and professional associations
items.text: Mandatory training and continuing professional development, with the need to show who took what, and when.

items.title: MOOCs and lifelong learning
items.text: Open courses with hundreds of participants and **lifelong learning** pathways, where nobody can follow each learner individually: the materials have to explain themselves, the self-assessments have to mark themselves, and the whole design _has to be reused for the next run, not rebuilt_.

sectors.note: In every one of these settings the requirement is the same: **a Moodle instance reachable over HTTPS and an AI assistant**. Nothing else changes.

usecases.title: What changes, and for whom
usecases.lead: One assistant, four ways of using it. The plugin applies each person's role: **those who may write, write; those who may only read, read**.

tabs.label: Teachers and trainers
tabs.intro: What sets MCPCA apart: not merely consulting Moodle, but ==building and maintaining the course through conversation==.

items.title: A whole course, from scratch
items.text: “Set up the ward safety course: eight sections, one per module, each with an introductory page and a self-assessment quiz.” The structure comes out of a single request, starting from an empty course; you then refine it section by section.

items.title: On a course that already exists
items.text: “Add a page on pain assessment scales, with a diagram, to section 4 and move the quiz to the end.” You work on what is already there, without redoing anything.

items.title: Well-formatted pages, not pasted text
items.text: “Turn these notes into a page in section 3.” The page comes out **laid out with the platform's styles**: paragraphs and subsections, lists, tables, formatted code, links, images and diagrams; longer lessons open with a clickable index. If requested, completion tracking is already on.

items.title: Quizzes in minutes
items.text: “Create 10 multiple-choice questions on the page ‘The stages of labour’, with feedback for every answer.” Questions in the bank, quiz in the course, pass mark set.

items.title: A different paper for every participant
items.text: “40 questions in the bank and a test that draws 10 of them at random.” Everyone gets a different combination and marking is automatic: the standard arrangement for an exam or an end-of-module test.

items.title: Automatically marked questions
items.text: Multiple choice, short answer, numerical with a tolerance (a drug dose calculation, for instance), Cloze with answers embedded in the text. Plus manually marked essays and descriptive blocks.

items.title: Materials in the right place
items.text: “Upload these slides to section 2 and have them open in a new window.” Files, labels, new or renamed sections, visibility.

items.title: Review and correction
items.text: “Read me the questions in the ‘Module 3’ category and fix the third one.” The question bank can be consulted and edited through conversation, with no menu hunting.

tabs.label: Instructional designers
tabs.intro: The people who design courses so that they reach **defined learning objectives**, usually working alongside the teacher or the subject matter expert. ==The page-building work moves to the assistant, and the time goes back into design.==

items.title: From the objective to the structure
items.text: “By the end of the module a participant must be able to calculate a paediatric dose: propose the sections, the materials and the assessments.” The design is discussed in words and published only once it convinces.

items.title: Assessment aligned to objectives
items.text: Every question is written against the learning outcome it measures. **An objective with no assessment**, or an assessment that measures nothing, shows up at once: the assistant reads the published course back and lists them.

items.title: Reviewing an existing course
items.text: “Read the course and tell me which sections have no self-assessment at all, and which materials no activity refers to.” _An analysis that takes hours when done by hand._

items.title: With the subject matter expert
items.text: The teacher provides the raw material — slides, notes, recordings — and the instructional designer turns it into a pathway. Getting from draft to published course **no longer goes through copy and paste**.

items.title: Templates to reapply
items.text: With Moodlecraft a course design becomes a text file: the same structure is reapplied to another module, another run or another department, with new content and new dates.

items.title: When there is no designer
items.text: Which is the common case. The same questions — which objectives, which prerequisites, how it will be assessed — can be put by the assistant to the teacher, and the course design drawn from the answers. _That is a way of running the conversation, not a feature of the plugin._

tabs.label: Students and learners
tabs.intro: **Always read-only**, and always only on the courses they are enrolled in.

items.title: Finding their way around
items.text: “Which courses am I enrolled in?” “What is in section 2?” Structure, materials and available quizzes, from the same Teams they use every day.

items.title: Explanations from the real course
items.text: “Explain the page on the stages of labour with an example.” The assistant reads what the teacher wrote and answers from that, without inventing.

items.title: Guided revision
items.text: “Test me on section 2.” Questions built from the course materials, with corrections and a pointer to the right page.

items.title: Their own results
items.text: “How did my last quiz go? What did I get wrong?” Grade, attempts and a review of their own answers. Their own only.

tabs.label: Organisation and IT
tabs.intro: For those who run the platform, those accountable for training, and those who must keep it under control.

items.title: Course structures in bulk
items.text: Creating categories and courses for a new term or a new run, updating settings and visibility en masse, reordering sections.

items.title: Quick checks
items.text: Who is enrolled in a course, the state of its activities, what a course contains ahead of a review or a migration.

items.title: Fine-grained control
items.text: Every tool can be switched off individually in the assistant: during a pilot, for example, the ones that delete content are disabled.

items.title: Traceability
items.text: Every call is an event in Moodle's log, with the user and the tool involved. No log to look for anywhere else.

features.lead: Everything below is **implemented and proven in the field**: the course described further down was built with these tools. Features still in development are listed in the next section.

items.title: Assignments and forums
items.text: Creating submissions and discussions from the conversation, as pages and quizzes already work today.

items.title: Learning analytics
items.text: Student progress and completion, queried from the conversation: “Who has not completed the mandatory module yet?” “Which questions in the last test had the most errors?”

items.title: From document to course
items.text: A Word or PDF file turned into a sequence of pages in the chosen section.

items.title: Deadlines for learners
items.text: “What do I have to hand in this week?” with dates and links to the activities.

items.title: H5P and other activities
items.text: Interactive **H5P** content — animations, interactive presentations, videos with embedded questions — generated from the conversation; then book and glossary.

items.title: Server-side two-step confirmation
items.text: Today the confirmation before each change is enforced by the assistant's instructions; it will become a constraint of the plugin itself.

dialogues.title: Sample conversations
dialogues.lead: Four representative exchanges, from university and healthcare training. The grey labels show which plugin tool the assistant used; readers not interested in the technical detail can ignore them. Before every change the assistant summarises the operation, asks for confirmation and only then carries it out.

items.title: A quiz built from a course page

Shall I go ahead?

items.title: An assessment with different questions for every participant

messages.text: For the Pharmacology assessment I want 40 questions in the bank covering modules 1–4, including dose calculation questions, and a test that draws 10 at random for each participant. Anyone below 6 does not pass.

items.title: Revision built on the lecturer's own materials

messages.text: Test me on section 2 of Physiology of Pregnancy and Childbirth.
Section 2 contains “The stages of labour” and “Care during the second stage”. First question: what are the stages of labour, and what marks the transition from the first to the second?
Dilation, expulsion and placental delivery. The second begins at full dilation.

Correct. The course page also distinguishes, within the first stage, the latent phase from the active phase. Second question: what is meant by the third stage, and within what interval is it expected under physiological conditions?

head: Question
What went wrong
rows: a `LEFT JOIN` also returns the rows of the left-hand table that have no match
a `CROSS JOIN` produces the Cartesian product

blocks.text: Would you like to go over outer joins using the example on the course page?

I cannot show other students' results. For comparisons and statistics, please ask your lecturer.

case_band.title: The first course built this way: databases for Midwifery
case_band.text: Laboratorio di Informatica, BSc in Midwifery at the University of Catania, academic year 2025/2026: **designing and querying a clinical database**, and building a small web application on top of it. Seven lessons, 73 pages, an exam bank of eighty questions and two papers with random draws, produced with MCPCA and Moodlecraft.
bullets: Lessons derived from slides and recorded videos, with an index and timestamps
Exercises and solutions on a clinical dataset of patients, births and staff
A different exam paper for every student, marked largely automatically

steps.title: From installation to the first conversation
steps.lead: Four steps, all on the side of whoever runs the systems. Teachers and learners install nothing: they find the assistant in Teams, or connect the MCP server to their own ChatGPT or Claude.

items.title: Install the plugin
items.text: Like any Moodle plugin, from site administration. Requires Moodle 4.3 or later.

items.title: Register the app in Entra ID
items.text: A supplied script creates the registration in the organisation's tenant. This is what enables sign-in with the Microsoft account.

items.title: Connect the server in Copilot Studio
items.text: Using the native MCP wizard: paste an address, choose which tools stay enabled, paste the supplied instructions.

items.title: Publish in Teams
items.text: The assistant appears in Teams and in Microsoft 365 Copilot for the chosen people: one department, a single course, the whole organisation.

security.title: Identity, permissions, data: the answers for whoever runs the systems
security.lead: The plugin does not add a permission system of its own: **it uses Moodle's, which the organisation already governs**.

items.title: Identity
items.text: Sign-in with the organisation's Microsoft account (Entra ID). It works only for people who have already signed in to Moodle through Microsoft at least once; **no account is created automatically**.

items.title: Authorisation
items.text: Moodle capabilities, **evaluated on every single call**. A teacher writes only in the courses where they teach; a learner never writes. The list of tools the assistant can see is filtered by role.

items.title: Data residency
items.text: The plugin runs inside Moodle and contacts no external service. The only third party is the chosen AI assistant: with Copilot, the organisation's own Microsoft tenant.

items.title: Traceability
items.text: Every call produces an event in Moodle's log, with user, tool and parameters. No log to consult outside the platform.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Every tool can be enabled or disabled individually in the assistant. In a pilot, the tools that delete content and those that expose third-party data are kept off.

items.title: Confirming changes
items.text: The assistant summarises what it is about to do and asks for confirmation, one change at a time. Anything it finds written inside course content is treated as **data, not as instructions**.

moodlecraft.title: The engine behind Moodlecraft: whole courses defined, versioned, reproducible
moodlecraft.lead: [[MCPCA]] is not only the bridge to AI assistants: it is also the engine on which [[Moodlecraft]] is built, a command-line tool that treats a Moodle course **as source code**: defined in text files, versioned, applicable to any Moodle instance where MCPCA is installed.

items.title: The course is a folder
items.text: One file with the course settings, one folder per section, pages in Markdown, quizzes and question banks in YAML, attachments alongside. All readable and editable with any editor.

items.title: Plan first, then apply
items.text: Like `Terraform` for cloud infrastructure: Moodlecraft compares the definition with the course as it stands on Moodle, shows what would change and applies only the differences. _Running it again duplicates nothing._

items.title: Versioned with git
items.text: Every change carries an author, a date and a reason. You can go back to an earlier version, work on the same course as a team, and review before publishing.

items.title: Reproducible
items.text: The same course on the test instance and on production, or ==replicated for the next run by changing only the dates==. Randomly drawn exam questions, diagrams and formatted code all come from the same definition.

moodlecraft.tree_title: A course, as Moodlecraft sees it
moodlecraft.note: The two approaches coexist: you can build the structure by talking to the assistant and then put it under version control with Moodlecraft, or define the course in files and leave the day-to-day edits to the assistant. The course in the case study was born exactly like this.

tech.title: Architecture and requirements
tech.lead: A Moodle web service plugin exposing **an MCP server**, plus a REST adapter and an OpenAPI specification for clients that do not speak MCP.

clients: Teams / M365 Copilot via Copilot Studio
VS Code, Cursor, other MCP clients
auth: or a Moodle web service token

specs.v: MCP Streamable HTTP, JSON-RPC 2.0. Negotiates versions 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26 and 2025-06-18.
Entra ID tokens validated for signature, issuer, audience and scope; the identity is resolved to the Moodle account linked through auth_oauth2. Alternatively, a Moodle web service token.
Dedicated capability webservice/mcpca:use; every tool checks the Moodle capabilities of the context (course, module). tools/list is filtered per user.
26 purpose-built tools (authoring: pages, sections, files, quizzes, questions, question bank) plus 22 native Moodle functions exposed as tools, 48 in total.
Copilot Studio verified (Teams and M365 Copilot). Any MCP client with OAuth or a token: Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor. REST and OpenAPI for ChatGPT Actions and custom integrations.
Moodle 4.3+, PHP 8.0+, HTTPS reachable from the cloud of the chosen assistant. No external services.
A privacy provider is declared; the plugin stores only the token's last access time and writes to Moodle's standard log.

tech.note: The code will be released under GPL v3, the same licence as Moodle. The link to the repository will appear here on publication.

items.q: Do I have to install anything on my computer?
items.a: No. The assistant appears as a chat in Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot, already in use in many organisations. Anyone who prefers ChatGPT or Claude connects the MCP server from their assistant's settings, signing in with their institutional account. Installation concerns only the Moodle server and the Copilot Studio configuration, both handled by whoever runs the systems.

No. It was born in a university, and that is where it was first proven, but **the plugin knows Moodle, not the sector**. Schools, healthcare organisations, accredited training providers and companies run the same Moodle and face the same problem: producing and keeping content and assessments up to date. The case study on this site is academic; the mechanisms it describes are the same everywhere.

items.q: Can I create a course from scratch?
items.a: Yes. Starting from an empty course, the assistant builds sections, pages, materials and assessments in a single conversation; or it works on a course that already exists. Creating the course container itself depends on permissions: in many organisations it is reserved to the administration, which sets it up in seconds. For courses you want to version and replicate for every run, there is [[Moodlecraft]].

items.q: Can a learner modify a course?
items.a: No. The plugin applies Moodle's permissions to every request: someone enrolled as a student can only consult the courses they are enrolled in. Even if they asked the assistant to create something, Moodle would refuse.

items.q: Where does course data end up?
items.a: It stays in Moodle. The plugin contacts no external service. Conversations pass through the chosen assistant: with Copilot, the organisation's Microsoft tenant that already hosts Teams and email.

Answers about courses are built by reading the real content through the plugin's tools, and the assistant's instructions require it to say when a piece of information is not in the course. As with any AI assistant, **whoever teaches still has to review what gets created**: that is why quizzes are born hidden.

Yes. Any MCP client can connect: ChatGPT and Claude through their own MCP connectors, VS Code, Cursor. Teams and Copilot are the recommended route because many organisations already have them and sign-in is the institutional one.

items.q: What is needed to try it?
items.a: A Moodle 4.3 or later reachable over HTTPS, Microsoft sign-in already enabled on Moodle, the Copilot Studio licences many organisations already hold, and a few hours from whoever runs the systems for the four steps described above. A pilot on a single course is the best way to start.

items.q: How much does it cost? Is it open source?
items.a: The code will be released under GPL v3, the same licence as Moodle, so there are no licence fees. During the pilot phase it is available on request to interested organisations.

The project is developed by Antonio Calanducci, computer engineer at the University of Messina and adjunct lecturer in Computer Science at the University of Catania, and was used to produce a real course, documented on the case study page. Reports and requests reach the address at the bottom of this page.

meta.title: Case study · Computing Lab in Midwifery, built with MCPCA
meta.description: How the Computing Lab of the BSc in Midwifery at the University of Catania was built with MCPCA and Moodlecraft: databases, SQL and a web application for clinical data, across seven lessons, with a question bank and exam papers.

case.title: Computing Lab in Midwifery: a course on databases and app development, built by conversation
case.lead: **Seven lab sessions**, _73 modules_, 21 hours, for third-year students of the BSc in Midwifery. They learn to design a relational database, to populate and query it with SQL and to build a small web application on top of it, working with data of various kinds. The working tools are **SQL** and **Oracle APEX**; the course is published on the _new Studium_, the University of Catania's **Moodle** portal. [[MCPCA]] and [[Moodlecraft]] made it possible to produce its lessons, exercises and exam papers: it is ==the first complete course produced with these tools==.

facts.v: Midwifery (qualifying for the profession of midwife), L/SNT1
Seven lab sessions, 21 hours, attendance required
Multiple-choice quiz and SQL exercises on healthcare data

link.label: Open the course on Studium
link.note: The course lives on the university platform: access requires UniCT credentials.

context.title: Databases inside a healthcare degree
paras: By the end of the course, a student must be able to **analyse a real information need in a healthcare professional setting** and to represent it, query it and evaluate it. This is data they will work with every day: patient records, the register of births, staff rotas. Students on the course will not become computer scientists, and the syllabus requires no programming background: ==they must be able to discuss data with the people who design the applications, and to retrieve the information they need on their own==.

The course is taught in person, in a computer lab, and is **mostly practical**: short explanations followed by individual exercises in Oracle APEX. Moodle provides the support: written lessons, screen recordings with transcripts, exercises. Preparing all that material is **the work that usually does not get done**, _because building and publishing it on Moodle by hand takes too many hours and too many steps_: at most, the slides get uploaded.

With MCPCA I described the intended result in words and obtained it in Moodle. With Moodlecraft the same course became **a folder of text files under git**: next year it is reapplied by changing the dates and the dataset, ==without starting over==.

metrics.note: Figures taken from the course on 27 July 2026, the last time its structure was mapped.

steps.title: From slide deck to exam paper, step by step
steps.lead: Each step is either a conversation with the assistant or a Moodlecraft command. The labels name the plugin tools used at that step.

items.title: From slides to lessons
items.text: Each lesson's slides became Markdown pages on Moodle: one topic per page, with tables, formatted code examples and summaries. Every lesson opens with a clickable index listing its pages in the order they should be followed.

items.title: From videos to pages with an index
items.text: The recorded lessons had transcripts. From those the assistant derived an index with timestamps and the text of each section: **not the raw transcript, but the content rewritten and condensed**, with the video always at the top of the page.

items.title: A storyline for the exercises
items.text: Lesson II is a detective case: a table of 500 suspects of various crimes and a series of clues to be turned into queries, narrowing the list down to a single name. Fifteen exercises and seventeen solutions, one page each, created alongside the text of the lesson.

items.title: The clinical dataset
items.text: For the exam exercises I used a dataset from the midwifery domain: patients, births, staff. The SQL file to work on is uploaded to the course as a downloadable resource, so everyone recreates the tables in their own Oracle APEX environment.

items.title: The question bank
items.text: One group of questions per lesson: twenty multiple-choice questions each, with written feedback for every wrong answer. **A fresh set is prepared for every exam session**, so anyone resitting does not meet the same questions again. They stay in the course bank and can be read back and corrected by conversation, without opening Moodle's editor.

items.title: The exam papers
items.text: Each paper draws twenty-two questions at random from the four banks — six from Lesson II, six from III, five from IV, five from V — and adds four practical exercises to be solved in Oracle APEX. Thirty marks in total and a pass at 60%, that is eighteen, as the syllabus prescribes; one attempt, one hour. Anyone who prefers can hand in a project instead: a small data-management application built in APEX.

items.title: The marking
items.text: Moodle marks the multiple-choice questions on its own, with feedback shown to the students. For the practical exercises I exported the answers to a spreadsheet, assessed them one by one with a mark and a comment, and imported them back into the gradebook: thirty-five scripts, eight answers each. _The export and re-import are currently handled by a project script._

items.title: The syllabus
items.text: The [course unit description published by the department](https://www.chirmed.unict.it/corsi/lsnt1/insegnamenti?seuid=DA193AB7-3EEF-41DC-8648-1D27BC1A586F) — intended learning outcomes, the contents of the seven lessons, assessment methods, reading list — also came out of the same material, by reading the published course instead of rewriting everything into a form: through [[MCPCA]] the AI assistant read the entire course and drafted the text, which was then published on **SmartEdu** by a dedicated script.

items.title: All of it versioned
items.text: The course is a folder under version control with git: `plan` shows what would change, `apply` applies only the differences.

index.heading: Lesson II — Introduction to SQL

mc.question: Which SQL clause or construct is used to combine the data of the patients and births tables on a shared key?

answers.feedback: GROUP BY groups rows for aggregate calculations, it does not link tables.
ORDER BY sorts the result, it does not link tables.
NOT negates a condition, it does not link tables.

mc.caption: One of the twenty questions in the Lesson III bank. The feedback explains why the wrong option is wrong.

questions.label: Exercise 2 — Query
questions.text: Write and run in Oracle APEX a query that, through a JOIN between the births and staff tables, returns the number of births attended by each midwife, ordered from the highest to the lowest.

questions.label: Exercise 2 — Result
questions.text: Report here the result you obtained by running the query for Exercise 2: the midwife's name and the corresponding count, in order.

open.note: Query and result are two separate questions, one mark each: getting the syntax wrong but reaching the right result does not cost the whole exercise.
open.caption: Four exercises like this one close the paper, on the dataset of patients, births and staff.

lessons.title: Six things I am taking to the next course
lessons.lead: Not everything worked the first time, and some choices have become rules.

items.title: The assistant does not invent the content
items.text: Pages come out of the real material: slides, transcripts, dataset. What it writes still has to be read back, and **responsibility for what gets published stays with whoever teaches**.

items.title: Marking stays a human decision
items.text: For the open exercises the assistant proposes a mark and a comment for each answer; I confirmed the final assessment myself, script by script, before entering it in the gradebook.

items.title: More than half of next year's work is already done
items.text: The course is a versioned folder: the dates, the dataset and the new questions change. The rest is reapplied in minutes, with the certainty that nothing is duplicated.

items.title: Time moves, it does not disappear
items.text: Building the pages of a course has become quick; the time has shifted to choosing what to ask for, reading back and correcting.

items.title: Students see none of this
items.text: They find a well-organised course, with an index per lesson, exercises with solutions and a different paper for each student. That it was built by conversation is a detail that concerns only its author.

items.title: Quizzes are born hidden
items.text: The second exam paper is declared hidden in the file that defines it, and every reapplication respects that choice.

cta.title: Interested in how it is built?
cta.text: I can show you the course, the files that generate it and how the exam papers were put together. If you teach or are responsible for training, one pilot course is enough to assess whether the approach suits your context.
